profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting at a multinational bank preparing a cross-functional briefing pack for the Executive Risk Committee on how pending AI regulations affect its fraud detection and credit decisioning programs. The meeting is between the Regulatory Affairs lead, who is assembling the legal/compliance section of the pack, and the Data Governance program manager, who is coordinating inputs from model owners and control teams. The agenda is to align on what goes into the shared jurisdiction matrix, who updates the risk landscape summary, which version of the AI inventory will be used, and what 'ready for committee' means by Thursday. The expected outcome is an apparently clear division of handoffs so the combined briefing can be circulated before the committee pre-read deadline.

members.name: Sonia Patel
members.role: Head of Regulatory Affairs for Digital Products
members.expertise: Financial regulation, policy interpretation, cross-jurisdiction compliance briefing
members.background: Former financial services lawyer who now translates emerging EU, UK, and US rules into internal governance guidance for senior leadership at a global bank.
members.private_state: She wants the committee pack to look stable and decision-ready, avoid reopening policy debates, and minimize last-minute caveats that could make her team appear reactive rather than in control.
hidden_assumptions: The 'jurisdiction matrix' is the executive summary table in PowerPoint that consolidates only externally applicable legal obligations by region.
'Current inventory' means the officially approved March 31 AI inventory snapshot, because frozen records are the only safe basis for executive-facing legal statements.
A 'risk landscape summary' for committee use should synthesize already-recognized risks and themes, not introduce intake-stage observations that have not been normalized through governance channels.
'Ready for committee' means the storyline, legal interpretation, and headline conclusions are stable enough for circulation, even if a few citations or confirmations are still pending.

members.name: Marcus Lee
members.role: Data Governance Program Manager for AI Controls
members.expertise: AI inventory management, control evidence collection, governance process coordination
members.background: Operations-oriented program manager who previously ran model risk reporting and now coordinates the bank's internal AI governance artifacts across business units.
members.private_state: He wants this committee cycle to reflect the operational reality on the ground, make teams work from the latest inventory data, and avoid his office being blamed later for omissions that were already visible in source systems.
hidden_assumptions: The 'jurisdiction matrix' is the working spreadsheet with rows for each AI use case and columns for legal, governance, data, and control impacts across regions.
'Current inventory' means the live April 8 export from the inventory tool, including new submissions and status changes not yet frozen into the month-end pack.
A 'risk landscape summary' naturally includes recent intake and assessment findings that help explain emerging exposure, even if those items are not yet formal enterprise risks.
'Ready for committee' means every artifact has owner-confirmed entries and traceable source links so no one is challenged on lineage or completeness during the session.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'finalize the jurisdiction matrix' for the committee pack.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a concise executive-facing slide summarizing major EU, UK, and US legal obligations at the jurisdiction level.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the detailed working spreadsheet mapping each AI use case to region-specific obligations, governance controls, and data dependencies.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts are genuinely called the jurisdiction matrix inside the bank, and in a coordination meeting it sounds natural to discuss ownership without re-specifying the format because each assumes the other is referencing the familiar standard artifact.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the committee materials should use the 'current inventory' of AI use cases.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the approved March 31 governance snapshot already circulated to Legal and Internal Audit.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the live April 8 export from the inventory tool that includes two newly flagged credit models and revised ownership tags.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are indeed referring to the organization's AI inventory and both call their version 'current'; the distinction between approved snapshot and live extract is routine process knowledge that neither expects to need to state explicitly in a short handoff discussion.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They align that Marcus will 'refresh the risk landscape summary' before Sonia folds it into the deck.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the task covers only tightening the narrative of recognized risk themes already accepted in governance forums, such as explainability, privacy, and third-party model oversight.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the task also includes adding newly surfaced intake-stage gaps, such as missing human-override documentation for a fraud model, because those items shape the current exposure picture even if they are not formally logged as enterprise risks.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'risk landscape summary' is broad enough to plausibly include either established risk themes or newly observed signals, and both see their interpretation as the obvious way to make the committee material more useful rather than as a change in scope.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the package needs to be 'ready for committee' by Thursday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this threshold is met once the storyline, conclusions, and legal positioning are stable enough for executive circulation, even if some citations and owner attestations come later.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this threshold requires each table entry to be owner-confirmed with source references and no unresolved placeholders in the shared files.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is a familiar milestone term used in many internal meetings, and both assume their standard of readiness is the obvious one because it usually goes unstated unless a deliverable is already visibly late.

turns.inner_thought: I need this pre-read to land as controlled and decision-ready. By Thursday, the storyline and legal conclusions need to be stable enough to circulate to the Executive Risk Committee, even if a few references are still being tidied in parallel. I do not want this meeting reopening substance.
turns.utterance: Thanks for jumping on. With the Executive Risk Committee pre-read going Thursday, I just want to confirm the handoffs on the AI regulation pack and make sure we're aligned on what needs to be ready for committee.

turns.inner_thought: She wants confidence on timing, so I should show the inputs are moving. Fraud and credit both sent updates, and model risk has filled in most of the outstanding items. If I consolidate everything in the shared workspace today, I can keep pushing owners for confirmations and source lineage. For me, ready for committee means the files can stand up to challenge.
turns.utterance: Yes, absolutely. I got an updated pass from fraud and credit this morning, and model risk has sent over most of what we were waiting on. I can line everything up in the shared workspace today so we're all working from the same set.

turns.inner_thought: My blocker is the executive summary table in PowerPoint that consolidates the external EU, UK, and US obligations. Once that jurisdiction matrix is settled, I can drop it into the deck and keep the regulatory narrative clean.
turns.utterance: Perfect. My main dependency is getting the jurisdiction matrix finalized so I can drop the EU, UK, and US comparison into the deck.

turns.inner_thought: She needs the working spreadsheet cleaned up. The jurisdiction matrix has use-case rows for fraud detection and credit decisioning that shifted this week, and I need those rows, control fields, and regional impacts straightened out before anything is reliable downstream.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I'll clean that up today, especially around the fraud detection and credit decisioning entries that changed this week.

turns.inner_thought: The legal section is anchored to the approved March 31 snapshot already seen by Legal and Internal Audit. I need us to stay with that current inventory so the baseline remains stable and I don't have to qualify the pack.
turns.utterance: That's helpful. The legal section is already keyed to the current inventory, so let's stick to that so the baseline stays consistent.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, we'll use the current inventory, meaning the live April 8 export once I reconcile the latest submissions and status changes. That gives us the exact baseline as of today, which is what I need if we're going to avoid being accused of missing visible items.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I'll pull the current inventory once the latest reconciliations are through so we have the exact baseline as of today.

turns.inner_thought: I also need a concise appendix page that sharpens the recognized themes already accepted through governance: explainability, privacy, third-party oversight, and similar items. The risk landscape summary should support my implications slide, not introduce new debates.
turns.utterance: And could you refresh the risk landscape summary as well? Keep it tight so I can append it behind the regulatory implications slide.

turns.inner_thought: Good, I can use that to include the recent intake-stage findings without saying so explicitly. The latest control assessments include the human-oversight documentation gap and some explainability issues, and those materially change the exposure picture even if they are not yet formal enterprise risks.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense. I'll make sure it reflects the latest control assessments so the themes come through clearly on explainability and human oversight.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds fine as long as this doesn't become a reason to delay circulation. Ready for committee means the narrative and conclusions are stable by Thursday afternoon; minor cleanup can follow without holding the pack.
turns.utterance: That's fine, as long as the pack is ready for committee by Thursday afternoon and we don't get held up by minor cleanup.

turns.inner_thought: I hear the timing, but I still need owner confirmations and source links in place. Otherwise the materials are exposed in committee. I'll push the owners today so the artifacts are genuinely ready for committee in my sense of the term.
turns.utterance: Understood. Thursday works. I'll chase the owners today so the files are ready for committee with confirmations and source links in place.

turns.inner_thought: Good. I'll hold the committee-facing narrative and keep the legal interpretation steady. Marcus just needs to update the executive comparison table and the supporting summary in the folder so I can assemble without reopening policy questions.
turns.utterance: Great. Then I'll handle the committee narrative, and you'll update the jurisdiction matrix and the risk landscape summary in the shared folder.

turns.inner_thought: That works. I'll send over the refreshed spreadsheet and summary once the live inventory is synced and the last owner responses are in. If I can close those gaps today, the package should be defensible end to end.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll send the refreshed materials over once the current inventory is synced and the remaining owner responses come in.
